list.listitem: Typical symptoms of Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) include fatigue, myalgias, spiking fever, headache, GI symptoms, and a characteristic rash at 2 to 4 or 5 days into the illness. C
There is a tick bite history in only about 50% of cases. C
Diagnosis is based on clinical grounds early in the illness. The best diagnostic test is the indirect immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) assay, which is retrospective. C
The drug of choice is doxycycline, with consideration of chloramphenicol during pregnancy. B
Early diagnosis and treatment are important because the disease has a high mortality rate if undiagnosed or diagnosed late. B

background.definition: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) is an infectious disease caused by the tick-borne bacterium Rickettsia rickettsii and has as part of its clinical features fever, headache, and a characteristic rash. It has a significant mortality rate if not treated in a timely fashion.

list.listitem: The average annual incidence during 1997 to 2002 was 2.2 cases per million persons. From 2000 to 2007, the annual reported incidence increased from 1.7 to 7 cases per million persons, and the average annual incidence from 2008-2012 was 8.9 cases per million.

From 2016 through 2017, there were unprecedented increases in all nationally-notifiable tickborne diseases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), with the largest percentage increase in cases of spotted fever rickettsiosis (from 4269 cases to 6248). Only 3% of cases, however, were confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays or demonstrated seroconversion; probable laboratory criterion is a single positive serology result, most often a single anti-Rickettsia IgG-positive result.

There is evidence that a single IgG antibody titer is unreliable evidence of spotted fever rickettsiosis. In one study of blood donors, 11.1% of donors from Georgia and 6.3% of donors from Oregon and Washington demonstrated antibody titers reactive with R. rickettsii at titers ≥64. Of 243 seropositive case patients interviewed, only 28% met inclusion criteria in the national case definition for spotted fever rickettsiosis.

Data from Indiana (2009 to 2016) showed both age and location differences in reported cases of tickborne disease. There were more Lyme disease diagnoses among Indiana residents 44 years of age or younger vs. older residents, and more cases of ehrlichiosis, RMSF, and tularemia reported in Indiana residents over age 44 years vs. younger residents. There were also significantly higher diagnoses reported in urban counties compared with rural or rural-mixed counties.

Incidence rates are especially high among American Indians with a CDC report noting an average annual RMSF incidence of 94.6 per million persons (increasing incidence trend from 24.2 in 2001 to 139.4 in 2008). This is believed to be due in part to the emergence of brown dog ticks as a vector in eastern Arizona. The average annual incidence on the three most affected reservations was 1360 cases per million (2009-2012).
In Sonora, Mexico, which borders Arizona, 1,129 cases and 188 RMSF deaths were reported during 2004-2015. In 2015 to 2018, 510 cases of RMSF were reported in this region.

Costs associated with cases of RMSF on two American Indian reservations (estimated population 20,000) between 2002 and 2011 included more than $1.3 million in acute medical costs, $181,100 in acute productivity lost due to illness, and $11.6 million in lifetime productivity lost from premature death.
The disease is more common in men.

RMSF is caused by the obligatory intracellular Gram-negative coccobacillus Rickettsia rickettsii. It is transmitted to humans in the eastern states by the American dog tick, Dermacentor variabilis, which is both the vector and main reservoir.

There were several species of spotted fever group rickettsiae other than R. rickettsii associated with illness among 10% of North Carolina residents who had acute and convalescent sera submitted for RMSF testing, suggesting that serologic testing using R. rickettsii antigen may miss cases. This finding is of unknown significance.

In Southern Arizona (2016-1017), serum and eschar swab specimens from 7 ill patients with tick bites, 4 of whom worked as Border Patrol agents, were evaluated for R. Rickettsia and R. parkeri; antibodies reactive to one or both antigens were detected in all patients.
RMSF is transmitted in the western states by the Rocky Mountain wood tick, D. andersoni.

In areas within Arizona, RMSF is transmitted by the brown dog tick Rhipicephalus sanguineus. Massive local infestations of this tick have resulted in an incidence of RMSF in the three most affected communities that is 150 times the U.S. national average.

Ticks become infected by feeding on the blood of infected animals, trans-stadially (stage to stage), or by transovarial (maternal body to eggs) passage. The ticks transmit the organism to humans by blood feeding.

In one study in Brazil, unfed nymphs and adult ticks had to be attached to the host guinea pig for >10 hours to transmit R. rickettsia; however, fed ticks needed a minimum of 10 minutes of attachment to transmit R. rickettsii to hosts.
The disease may also be transmitted to humans when the tick is removed and crushed between the fingers, when one may be exposed to infective tick hemolymph.

The changing epidemiology of tick- and mosquito-borne diseases in recent decades appears related to climate change. RMSF incidence has spread to new Midwestern US geographic areas. This appears to be influenced by poverty status, average relative humidity, and average land surface temperature (>35°C) in the region.
There has also been a case of accidental needle-stick transmission of RMSF in Brazil; both the patient and nurse died.
The incubation period is 3 to 12 days.

Once the bacteria enter the body through the tick bite, they apparently spread via lymphatics and small blood vessels to invade the endothelial and smooth muscle cells of blood vessels in many organs and cause generalized vascular injury. The bacteria also spread through the systemic and pulmonary circulations.

The major effect of the bacteria on endothelial cells is to cause increased vascular permeability that results in edema, hypovolemia, hypotension, and hypoalbuminemia. This may progress to congestive heart failure and acute respiratory distress syndrome in severe cases.
Use long-sleeved clothing while in endemic areas and tuck pants into socks. C

Use tick repellants (DEET) on skin and permethrin on clothing. C Use of long-lasting permethrin-impregnated clothing that allows clothing to retain insecticidal activity for over 70 washes was shown to reduce the incidence of tick bites in a small pilot study of 16 outdoor workers.
Carefully and completely remove ticks with forceps by grasping ticks close to the skin and using steady upward traction. Then wash the site with soap and water. C
Perform frequent checks of the entire body for ticks. C

In one 2-year pilot study, use of long-acting tick collars on all dogs in the community, environmental acaricides applied monthly to yards, and encouragement of animal care practices such as spay and neuter and proper tethering procedures resulted in a marked reduction of visible tick infestations on dogs in intervention vs. control communities (<1% with sustained tick control of <3% vs. 64%, respectively).

Similarly, a community intervention including long-acting acaricidal collars on dogs, environmental acaricides applied to peri-domestic areas, and RMSF education led to a reduction in prevalence of tick-infested dogs from 32.5% to 8.8% and no new cases of RMSF during the subsequent 18 months compared to the neighboring control community which experienced a nonsignificant drop in percentage of tick-infested dogs in from 19% to 13.4% and two cases of reported RMSF, including one death.
Prophylactic antibacterial therapy is not recommended for those with recent tick bites or who are seropositive but are not ill.
Understanding the changing spacial distribution of the ticks and their hosts will assist in developing actions to prevent the associated diseases.
Diagnosis is usually based at first on clinical features. C
Maintain a high index of suspicion in endemic areas, remembering that the disease may also occur in nonendemic areas. C
Early manifestations are fatigue, myalgias, spiking fever, severe headache, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. C
The typical rash appears 2 to 4 or 5 days after onset of fever. C
IFA is the most accurate test, but it requires acute and convalescent titers. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Coryza and conjunctivitis are unusual in RMSF. The rash is more edematous in RMSF and almost never starts on the face, as it does in measles
The rashes of both these diseases may be petechial at one point, but the rash of meningococcemia becomes purulent and necrotic earlier
The abdominal pain associated with gastroenteritis is usually less severe than with RMSF, and rash is rare with the former
The rash is maculopapular and petechial, but, unlike RMSF, it spares the hands and feet

list.listitem: Most cases are seen during the late spring and summer, especially in residents or visitors to the South Atlantic states, the East South Central states, and the Rocky Mountain states. However, cases of RMSF on American Indian reservations in Arizona appear to occur year-round and peak later (July-September) than RMSF cases reported from other US regions.

Ask about contact with pets, especially dogs with ticks; RMSF in family members; illness in the family dog (e.g., fever, lethargy, decreased appetite); and recent (within 2 weeks) travel to an endemic area including Arkansas, Missouri, North Carolina, Oklahoma, and Tennessee.

The typical patient presents with spiking fever, severe headache, myalgias, nausea, and malaise. A history of tick bite within 14 days of illness onset is reported in 55% to 60% of RMSF cases but is not required for diagnosis.

The typical rash appears 2 to 4 or 5 days after the onset of fever. It starts around wrists and ankles and is red and macular, blanching to pressure. It later becomes petechial and moves to the palms, soles, trunk, and head.

Ocular findings are common, presenting as vasculitis of the conjunctiva, retina and choroid. Manifestations can include cotton wool spots, macular edema, retinal artery or vein occlusion and intraretinal hemorrhages and exudates that can result in vision loss. Less common associated conditions include optic neuritis, ischemic optic neuropathy and anterior uveitis.
Less common features include severe abdominal pain associated with GI signs or meningeal signs or encephalitis. Inflammatory polyarticular arthritis has also been reported.
Late in the course of untreated disease, manifestations can include cutaneous necrosis and gangrene, focal neurologic deficits, and renal failure.
An eschar may be present at the tick site.
Typical features of RMSF compared with those of other tick-borne diseases are shown in .

Obtain a CBC, metabolic panel, and peripheral blood smear. (While RMSF will not show up in the peripheral smear, it may be helpful in identifying or eliminating other causes of symptoms.) Common laboratory findings include thrombocytopenia, slightly elevated white blood cell count with increased immature neutrophils, slightly increased hepatic transaminase, and hyponatremia.
Leukopenia and elevated transaminases are common. The platelet count is low in about 33% of patients. Disseminated intravascular coagulation occurs in severe cases.
Serum sodium is commonly low due to inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone, seen in 20% of cases.
CSF analysis may show lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein.

IFA is the most specific and sensitive test. Acute and convalescent titers should be drawn. A diagnostic titer is 1:64 or greater.In one study, however, although antibodies to R. rickettsii were detected in 10 (77%) patients using a standard IFA assay, in nearly half the patients, IgM antibodies were observed without a corresponding development of IgG, and recent infection with a spotted fever group rickettsiae could not be confirmed for any patient.
Rickettsii may be isolated in blood cultures. However, the technique for isolation is complex and is only done in a few laboratories.
In addition, low numbers of rickettsiae typically circulate in blood in the absence of advanced disease, making PCR tests less useful.
Rickettsii may also be seen in cutaneous biopsies of the rash, but only a few hospitals and public health laboratories are able to perform the proper techniques for this procedure.
Multiplex real-time PCR can be an effective method to specifically identify cases of RMSF, rickettsialpox, and R. parkeri rickettsiosis using skin biopsy specimens.

Particularly in endemic areas, consider RMSF in patients with fatigue, myalgias, spiking fever, severe headache, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea in the absence of upper respiratory symptoms. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are critical to survival.

The characteristic rash starts around the wrists and ankles and is red and macular, blanching to pressure. It later becomes petechial. Ask about a history of recent tick bite which is positive in about 50% of cases.

Draw acute and convalescent IFA titers to confirm the diagnosis. If bacterial meningitis, especially meningococcal disease, cannot be ruled out, give IM ceftriaxone in addition to oral doxycycline, followed by inpatient observation.
RMSF is a nationally notifiable disease in the US, and health providers should notify the state or local health department.
Prompt treatment with doxycycline is recommended for all tickborne rickettsial diseases in children and adults. A
The antibiotic of choice is doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours in nonpregnant adults. B
The dose for children weighing less than 100 lb (45.4 kg) is 2.2 mg/kg/dose every 12 hours; the potential for lethality outweighs the possibility of teeth staining in children. B
Treat for 3 days after the fever subsides and until evidence of clinical improvement is noted (minimum 5-7 days). B
An alternate antibiotic is tetracycline 25 to 50 mg/kg/d orally or IV. C
The antibiotic of choice is doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours in adults.
The dose for children weighing less than 100 lbs is 2.2 mg/kg/dose given every 12 hours.

Antibiotic is administered for 3 days after the fever subsides and until evidence of clinical improvement is noted, which is usually means a minimum total course of 5 to 7 days. It may be given IV if the patient is vomiting.
Persistent fever after 48 hours should prompt consideration of alternative or additional diagnoses.
The second antibiotic of choice is tetracycline 25 to 50 mg/kg/d either orally or IV.

Limited courses of doxycycline or tetracycline do not pose a significant threat of tooth staining in children; the risk of lethality of disease outweighs concerns about teeth staining in children.In a study of 58 children treated with an average of 1.8 courses of doxycycline before 8 years of age and who now had exposed permanent teeth, no tetracycline-like staining was observed in those teeth.
Rickettsii is sensitive in vitro to rifampin, ciprofloxacin, and clarithromycin. However, there is insufficient clinical experience with these drugs to recommend their use in RMSF.
The patient may require vigorous fluid resuscitation due to increased vascular permeability, and intensive care if severely ill.
Follow the patient daily if not hospitalized or hospitalize the patient.
Report potential cases to the health department.
Consult with a pediatric or adult infectious disease specialist if the diagnosis is at all in question.
Hospitalize for IV medications if the patient is judged to be severely ill, especially if he or she is vomiting.
Hospitalize if there is any suspicion by the physician that the patient may not take her/his antibiotics.
Consider consulting a nephrologist for patients in acute renal failure.
Consult an intensivist if the patient is extremely ill.

Meningoencephalitis is a potential complication of spotted fever rickettsioses. In a case series of 11 children and 8 adults, rash was more commonly seen in children (100% vs. 50%) and all children but no adults were found to have multifocal, punctate diffusion restricting or T2 hyperintense lesions on MRI. Ninety percent required intensive care, 39% were intubated and just under half (46%) had made a complete recovery by hospital discharge.
The mortality rate has been reported to be as high as 20% if the patient is not treated appropriately and 1% to 3% if treated appropriately. B
The highest US case fatality rates of 7% to 10% are among American Indian communities in Arizona. Case fatality rates in Sonora, Mexico for children aged <10 years are as high as 30%.

The case fatality rate reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) remained unchanged from 1999 to 2007 at <1%. Of the 40 cases (40/7738 cases; 0.5%) reported to the CDC over that time period, causes of death included septicemia, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, central nervous system disorders, and renal failure .

Associated risk factors for death included American Indian ethnicity vs. white (relative risk [RR] = 3.9), age 5-9 years (RR = 6.0) or ≥70 years (RR = 3.0) vs. other ages, and immunosuppression (RR = 4.4). In another study, doxycycline was initiated significantly later in fatal vs. nonfatal cases (median, day 7 vs. day 3). Factors in this study that increased the risk of doxycycline delay and fatal outcome were early symptoms of nausea and diarrhea, history of alcoholism or chronic lung disease, and abnormal laboratory results such as elevated liver aminotransferases.
In Sonora, Mexico, of 510 cases of RMSF reported, 252 (49%) were in persons aged ≤18 years. Case fatality rate was 44%. Older age and being confirmed by PCR were associated with mortality.
Additional risk factors for more fulminant disease are alcohol abuse, glucose-6-phophate dehydrogenase deficiency, and initial treatment with a sulfonamide.
Surviving patients may lose digits and occasionally limbs due to ischemic necrosis. B
Neurologic signs (seizure or coma), acute renal failure, and acute respiratory distress syndrome indicate a poor prognosis. B
CNS abnormalities including ataxia, hyperreflexia, and overall decrease in cognitive ability may persist for up to one month after resolution. C
Possible long-term sequelae include bowel and bladder incontinence, difficulty with language, and impairment of cerebellar, vestibular, and motor functions. C
Keep the index of suspicion high and the treatment aggressive in older persons since they have the highest mortality rate.
The disease may occur without the rash in older and black patients ("Rocky Mountain spotless fever").
Antibiotic options during pregnancy are tetracycline or chloramphenicol (50 to 75 mg/kg/d).

There are limited data about tetracycline-associated risks of malformation of teeth and bones in the fetus but hepatotoxicity in the mother has not been seen with doxycycline. Chloramphenicol use late during the third trimester is associated with a theoretical risk for gray baby syndrome – lack of ability to metabolize the drug resulting in hypotension, hypothermia, gastrointestinal symptoms and gray skin color. Risk of maternal death is higher following use of chloramphenicol.

Four pregnant women in Sonora, Mexico who presented with fever and a petechial rash were identified with RMSF during 2015-2016 and successfully treated with doxycycline. The three women treated during their first trimester suffered spontaneous abortions and the final woman delivered a healthy infant at 36 weeks gestation.
Short-term use of doxycycline is likely safe during breastfeeding although small amounts are excreted in breast milk.
Children under age 15 years with RMSF are more likely to have a rash and develop the rash earlier in the course of illness compared to adults.
The dose for children weighing less than 100 lbs is 2.2 mg/kg/dose given every 12 hours.

Similar to adults, delay in initiating doxycycline (≥5th day from onset; OR(adj) 2.62, 95% CI 1.24-5.52), low platelet count (<50,000/μL), acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage increase risk of mortality.

Rickettsia rickettsii (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) Dermacentor variabilis (American dog tick), Dermacentor andersoni (Rocky Mountain wood tick), and Rhipicephalus sanguineus (brown dog tick) in Arizona Widespread in the United States, especially South Atlantic and South Central states 3-12 Fever, nausea, vomiting, myalgia, anorexia, and headache Thrombocytopenia, mild hyponatremia, and mildly elevated hepatic transaminase levels Maculopapular rash approximately 2-4 days after fever onset in 50%-80% of adults (>90% in children); might involve palms and soles 5-10
Ehrlichia chaffeensis (human monocytotropic ehrlichiosis) Amblyomma americanum (lone star tick) South and Mid-Atlantic, North/South Central United States, and isolated areas of New England 5-14 Fever, headache, malaise, and myalgia Leukopenia, thromobocytopenia, and elevated serum transaminase levels Rash in <30% of adults and approximately 60% of children 2-3
Anaplasma phagocytophilum (human granulocytotropic anaplasmosis) Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes pacificus (blacklegged tick) in the United States New England, North Central and Pacific states 5-21 Fever, headache, malaise, myalgia, and vomiting Leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, elevated serum transaminase levels Rare <1
Ehrlichia ewingii infection Amblyomma americanum (lone star tick) South Atlantic and South Central United States to isolated areas of New England 5-14 Fever, headache, myalgia, nausea, and vomiting Leukopenia, thromobocytopenia, and elevated serum transaminase levels Rare No documented fatalities
Treatment for each of these diseases is the same: adults, doxycycline 100 mg orally or IV twice daily; and children, doxycycline 2.2 mg/kg administered orally or IV twice daily.
